advances: The endpoint permits different density constants and may require a new hidden coordinate. The last observation concerns original-space support dimension, without assuming different fibers' support directions agree.

proof:
By Borell's endpoint characterization in [Fradelizi and Guédon, §2, p. 329](https://perso.math.u-pem.fr/fradelizi.matthieu/pdf/localizationDCG.pdf), the densities are constant on convex supports. Positive finite mass forces the supports bounded: an unbounded full-dimensional convex support contains disjoint equal-radius midpoint balls obtained using a fixed interior ball and escaping support points. The cross inequality applied to shrinking balls about source support points gives the support inclusion. For interior points $x_i\in Q_{z_i}$ take balls of radii $\varepsilon a_i$ at the inputs, $a_i>0$, with $\varepsilon$ so small that all input balls and their Minkowski average lie in the corresponding interiors. The normalized inequality is
$$
c_j^{1/m}\sum_i\lambda_i a_i\ge\sum_i\lambda_i c_{z_i}^{1/m}a_i .
$$
Letting all but one radius factor tend to zero shows $c_j\ge c_{z_i}$ for each $i$. Conversely use the support inclusion to replace each $E_i$ by $E_i\cap Q_{z_i}$ inside the target support, then apply $m$-dimensional Brunn–Minkowski and use $c_j\ge c_{z_i}$ in each term. This proves the inequality for the original test sets.

The supports may be the same interval at bases $-1,0,1$ with constants $1,2,1$ (or the same convex body in any dimension). Every nontrivial anchored combination uses the central target, and the criterion holds. If all constants equal $c$, the supports carry exactly the common-scaled ordinary volumes. In general, $c_j\ge\max_i c_{z_i}$ implies $[0,\sum_i\lambda_i c_{z_i}]\subseteq[0,c_j]$, so the prisms have the required Minkowski inclusions and project their ordinary $(m+1)$-volume to the given densities.

Finally, suppose a positive limit law from common normalization has full support dimension in the original $\mathbb R^m$. Its prelimit fiber volumes are bounded by the total mass tending to zero. Select a Hausdorff-convergent subsequence of those bounded compact convex fibers; they are nonempty eventually by positivity of the weak limit mass. The limiting convex set contains the support of the weak law, since a neighborhood disjoint from the limit is eventually disjoint from the fibers. It is therefore full dimensional, so volume continuity contradicts the vanishing volumes.

statement:
Let $\nu_z$ be finite positive $1/m$-concave measures of full affine support dimension $m$ in $\mathbb R^m$, so $\nu_z=c_z\mathbf1_{Q_z}\,dx$ on compact convex bodies $Q_z$. For an anchored combination $j=\sum_i\lambda_i z_i$ with $\lambda_i>0$ and $\sum_i\lambda_i=1$, the cross inequality
$$
\nu_j\Bigl(\sum_i\lambda_i E_i\Bigr)^{1/m}\ge\sum_i\lambda_i\nu_{z_i}(E_i)^{1/m}
$$
on compact positive-source-mass sets is equivalent to $Q_j\supseteq\sum_i\lambda_iQ_{z_i}$ and $c_j\ge\max_i c_{z_i}$. The constants need not coincide. A common multiplier on the original supports works when they coincide; otherwise the prisms $Q_z\times[0,c_z]$ give compatible $(m+1)$-volume lifts. In a bounded prelimit actual $m$-fiber sequence with total ordinary volume tending to zero, a positive surviving fiber cannot have a full-dimensional limit law in its original continuous space.
title: Full-dimensional endpoint of cross-measure Brunn–Minkowski
